sec.title: Background
sec.p: Patients with HER2-negative advanced breast cancer (ABC) have limited chemotherapy options after progression on anthracyclines and taxanes. Mitoxantrone Hydrochloride Liposome (Lipo-MIT), a nanoparticle formulation with a 60-nm particle size, is designed to reduce toxicity and enhance tumor targeting. We investigated the safety and efficacy of Lipo-MIT combined with capecitabine in pretreated HER2-negative ABC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this phase I dose-escalation study, eligible patients were sequentially enrolled to receive escalating doses of Lipo-MIT (ranging from 16 to 24 mg/m2) administered either every 3 weeks (Q3W) or every 4 weeks (Q4W), combined with standard capecitabine. Primary endpoints included dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) and determination of the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). Secondary endpoints assessed safety and preliminary efficacy.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Twenty-six patients were enrolled. Lipo-MIT 22 mg/m2 administered Q4W was identified as the RP2D. The combination demonstrated a manageable safety profile, with no reports of severe cardiac toxicity or hand-foot syndrome. Interstitial lung disease was observed in 19.2% of patients, all of which were manageable and low-grade (Grade 1–2). In a post hoc, exploratory analysis, the objective response rate (ORR) was 36.4% in the Q4W cohort and 13.3% in the Q3W cohort. The Q4W regimen yielded a median progression-free survival (mPFS) of 12.7 months (95% CI, 9.3–NR), which was numerically longer than the mPFS of 5.4 months observed in the Q3W cohort, albeit in the context of a sequential design and baseline imbalances.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The combination of Lipo-MIT and capecitabine showed preliminary antitumor activity and manageable tolerability in heavily pretreated HER2-negative ABC. While the Q4W dosing schedule (22 mg/m²) yielded numerically longer PFS, this comparison is based on a non-randomized, sequential cohort design; thus, all inter-cohort efficacy findings are strictly exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Further evaluation in phase II/III trials as a potential later-line strategy.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Breast cancer remains the most diagnosed malignancy and the leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide [1]. Approximately 60–70% of metastatic breast cancer cases are human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative [2]. For patients with HER2-negative advanced breast cancer (ABC), sequential chemotherapy remains the cornerstone of palliative treatment, particularly after progression on endocrine therapy or for those with visceral crisis. While anthracyclines and taxanes represent the standard first-line cytotoxic agents, virtually all patients eventually develop resistance [3, 4]. Following the failure of these key therapeutic classes, there is currently no globally established standard-of-care chemotherapy regimen. Consequently, the prognosis for this heavily pretreated population remains poor, underscoring an urgent unmet need for novel, effective, and tolerable therapeutic strategies.

Mitoxantrone, an anthraquinone antibiotic antitumor drug, has historically demonstrated potent antitumor activity in breast cancer by intercalating into deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and inhibiting topoisomerase II [5, 6]. However, its clinical utility has been severely restricted by cumulative dose-dependent cardiotoxicity and myelosuppression [7, 8]. To overcome these pharmacological limitations, Mitoxantrone Hydrochloride Liposome (Lipo-MIT) was developed. This novel formulation encapsulates mitoxantrone within pegylated liposomes, significantly altering the drug’s pharmacokinetic profile [9]. Through the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, Lipo-MIT preferentially accumulates in tumor tissues while reducing distribution to normal tissues, notably the myocardium [10, 11]. This formulation aims to maintain or enhance efficacy while mitigating the severe adverse events associated with the free drug, thereby mitigating off-target toxicities, particularly cardiotoxicity [12]. Preclinical and early-phase clinical studies have demonstrated that Lipo-MIT exhibits a favorable safety profile and promising antitumor activity in solid tumors [12, 13].

Capecitabine, an oral fluoropyrimidine, is a widely utilized agent in the metastatic setting, particularly for patients previously treated with anthracyclines and taxanes. Its mechanism of action—enzymatic conversion to fluorouracil preferentially within tumor cells—offers a favorable safety profile and the convenience of oral administration [14]. Preclinical and clinical data suggest that combining DNA-damaging agents with antimetabolites can yield synergistic antitumor effects [15, 16]. Given the distinct toxicity profiles of Lipo-MIT and capecitabine, their combination holds promise as a viable salvage therapy; however, the optimal dosing strategy and safety profile of this doublet remain to be established.

Here, we report the results of a phase I, dose-escalation study designed to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and preliminary efficacy of Lipo-MIT combined with capecitabine in patients with HER2-negative ABC who have failed at least one prior line of systemic therapy.

sec.title: Ethical statement
sec.p: The present study (protocol number: CSPC-DED-BC-K01) was approved by the Ethics Committee of the National Cancer Center/Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College (Approval No. 23/123-3865) and was registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06156761, www.clinicaltrials.gov). The study design and conduct complied with all relevant regulations regarding the use of human study participants and was conducted in accordance with the criteria set by the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations. All patients voluntarily participated and provided written informed consent before the initiation of any study-related treatment or procedures.

sec.title: Study design and treatment schedule
sec.p: The present study was an open-label, multiple-dose, phase I dose-escalation trial in patients with HER2-negative ABC, incorporating two dosing schedules (3-week [Q3W] and 4-week [Q4W] cycles) to optimize treatment intensity and tolerability. The primary objectives were to assess safety and efficacy, and to identify the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of Lipo-MIT.

The study employed a standard “3+3” dose-escalation design based on dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) observed during Cycle 1. If the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was not reached, the RP2D was determined through a holistic clinical assessment by the Safety Review Committee (SRC). This comprehensive evaluation incorporated the incidence of cumulative toxicities, the necessity for dose modifications, definitive treatment discontinuations, and relative dose intensity across all treatment cycles.

Patients were enrolled sequentially. The Q3W cohort was enrolled first; subsequently, guided by emerging clinical safety data supporting the need for extended hematopoietic recovery and the known prolonged plasma half-life of Lipo-MIT, a protocol amendment was implemented to assign subsequent patients to the Q4W cohort. Trial-specific pharmacokinetic analyses are currently ongoing and will be reported in a separate publication.

Lipo-MIT was administered intravenously on day 1 of each cycle, with dose escalation ranging from 16 to 22 mg/m². Capecitabine was administered orally at fixed doses: 1000 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–14 for the 3-week schedule, and 825 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–21 for the 4-week schedule. Treatment continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal of consent, or investigator decision. The study design and dose-escalation scheme are illustrated in Figure 1.Fig. 1

Eligible patients with HER2-negative advanced breast cancer were assigned to either a 3-week or 4-week cycle cohort receiving Lipo-MIT combined with capecitabine. A standard “3 + 3” design was utilized to escalate Lipo-MIT doses from 16 to 22 mg/m² to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoints were the incidence of DLTs during the first treatment cycle, determination of the MTD, and identification of the RP2D of Lipo-MIT when combined with capecitabine. The DLT observation window was defined as the first cycle of treatment (21 days for the Q3W schedule and 28 days for the Q4W schedule). DLTs were graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI CTCAE) version 5.0 and defined as treatment-related events including: grade 4 neutropenia lasting >3 days or resistant to G-CSF; grade ≥3 febrile neutropenia; grade 3 thrombocytopenia with bleeding or requiring transfusion; grade 4 anemia; grade ≥2 reduction in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF); or grade ≥3 non-hematological toxicities. Exceptions were made for transient (≤24 h) grade 3 constitutional symptoms (e.g., fever, fatigue) or manageable grade 3 gastrointestinal/metabolic toxicities resolving to grade ≤1 within 48 h. The MTD was defined as the highest dose level at which <33% (e.g., <2 of 6) of patients experienced a DLT.

Secondary endpoints included overall safety, characterized by the incidence and severity of treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs), which were defined as those assessed by the investigator as possibly, probably, or definitely related to the study drug; antitumor activity assessed by overall response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR), evaluated according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1; and progression-free survival (PFS).

PFS was defined as the time from the first dose of the study drug to the first documented objective tumor progression per RECIST v1.1 or death from any cause. In accordance with the intention-to-treat principle, treatment discontinuation due to toxicity was not considered a PFS event. Patients who discontinued treatment for reasons other than disease progression continued to undergo scheduled tumor assessments until documented progression, death, or initiation of a new anti-cancer therapy. Patients were censored only at the last evaluable tumor assessment if they were alive and progression-free at the data cutoff, or if they were lost to follow-up.

sec.title: Patient eligibility
sec.p: Eligible patients were females aged 18 to 70 years with histologically confirmed HER2-negative ABC (immunohistochemistry [IHC] 0, 1+, or 2+/in situ hybridization [ISH]-negative). Patients were required to have hormone receptor-negative disease, or hormone receptor-positive disease that was resistant to or unsuitable for endocrine therapy. Patients must have experienced disease progression after at least one line of systemic therapy in the metastatic setting, with prior exposure to anthracyclines or taxanes. For patients who received adjuvant anthracyclines, the recurrence-free interval was required to be >12 months. Additional inclusion criteria included an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of 0–1, a LVEF ≥50%, and adequate organ function.

Key exclusion criteria included prior treatment with mitoxantrone or liposomal formulations; cumulative prior doxorubicin dose >350 mg/m2 or epirubicin >700 mg/m2; and receipt of any anti-tumor therapy within 4 weeks before enrollment. Patients with uncontrolled brain metastases, active hepatitis B/C, or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection were excluded. Strict cardiac exclusion criteria applied to patients with a corrected QT interval (QTc) >480ms, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class ≥II heart failure, or significant history of arrhythmia or myocardial infarction within 6 months.

sec.title: Efficacy and safety assessment
sec.p: Tumor response was assessed by investigators using computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) according to RECIST v1.1. Radiological assessments were performed at screening (within 28 days prior to enrollment) , every 2 cycles during the treatment period , and at the end of treatment or withdrawal.

Safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose of the study drug. Adverse events were monitored continuously from informed consent until 21 days (3-week cohort) or 28 days (4-week cohort) after the last dose, with severity graded according to NCI CTCAE v5.0. Hematological parameters were monitored weekly during the first cycle. Cardiac monitoring included 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) and cardiac biomarkers (troponin I/T, BNP/NT-ProBNP) at the beginning of each cycle, and echocardiography for LVEF assessment every 2 cycles. Furthermore, to monitor for potential delayed cardiotoxicity, comprehensive cardiac evaluations (including ECG, LVEF, and biomarker assessments) were strictly mandated at the End of Treatment (EOT) safety visit, conducted 21 days (for the Q3W cohort) or 28 days (for the Q4W cohort) after the last administered dose. Subsequent post-treatment cardiac monitoring was conducted as clinically indicated.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 29.0.1.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Graphical visualizations and exploratory multivariable Cox proportional hazards model were generated using R (version 4.2.2) within RStudio (version 2025.09.2+418), specifically utilizing the survival package for all survival estimates and Cox regression models, and the survminer package for generating Kaplan-Meier curves.

The safety analysis set included all patients who received at least one dose of the study drug, while the full analysis set (FAS) comprised all enrolled patients. The primary pre-specified objectives of this Phase I study were to evaluate safety, tolerability, and determine the MTD and RP2D. The sample size was determined by the dose-escalation algorithm and was not based on a formal statistical power calculation. Missing clinical and safety data were not imputed and were analyzed as observed. Baseline characteristics and safety data were summarized using descriptive statistics, including frequencies and percentages for categorical variables, and means (with standard deviations) or medians (with ranges) for continuous variables. Regarding efficacy endpoints, the ORR and DCR were summarized as percentages, with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) calculated using the Clopper-Pearson exact method. PFS was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and median survival times along with 95% CIs were reported, with CIs calculated based on the log transformation. Furthermore, the median follow-up duration was determined using the reverse Kaplan-Meier method.

Because the study was non-randomized and not prospectively powered for efficacy comparisons, all inter-cohort efficacy analyses (Q3W vs. Q4W) were conducted post hoc and are considered purely exploratory. An exploratory log-rank test was performed to compare the Kaplan-Meier PFS curves between cohorts. Furthermore, given the baseline imbalances between the Q3W and Q4W cohorts, an exploratory multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was performed to estimate the adjusted hazard ratio and corresponding 95% CIs, adjusting for potential confounders, including hormone receptor (HR) status, prior cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitor exposure, and the number of prior lines of therapy. In this model, covariates were coded as follows: hormone receptor status as a binary variable (positive vs. negative), prior CDK4/6 inhibitor exposure as a binary variable (yes vs. no), and prior lines of therapy as a continuous variable.

sec.title: Study population and baseline characteristics
sec.p:
From June 2023 to January 2025, a total of 26 eligible patients with HER2-negative ABC were enrolled in the study. The study population was categorized into two cohorts: 15 patients received Lipo-MIT every 3 weeks (Q3W) combined with capecitabine, and 11 patients received Lipo-MIT every 4 weeks (Q4W) combined with capecitabine. The median age of the total population was 56.5 years (range: 35–66). Regarding HR status, 65.4% (17/26) of patients were HR-positive, while 34.6% (9/26) were HR-negative. In terms of HER2 expression, 38.5% (10/26) of patients were classified as HER2 IHC 0. The remaining 61.5% (16/26) exhibited HER2-low status (defined as IHC 1 + or IHC 2+/ISH-negative), comprising 38.5% (10/26) with IHC 1 + and 23.1% (6/26) with IHC 2+/ISH-negative tumors. Specifically, the proportion of HER2-low patients was 66.7% (10/15) in the Q3W cohort and 54.5% (6/11) in the Q4W cohort.

The patients had a considerable tumor burden at baseline, with 61.5% presenting with visceral metastases and 53.8% with bone metastases. Regarding treatment history in the metastatic setting, the median number of prior systemic therapy lines was 2 (range: 1–4). Specifically, 38.5% of patients had received 1 prior line, while 61.5% had received 2 or more prior lines. Notably, the Q4W cohort represented a more heavily pre-treated population (median 3 lines) compared to the Q3W cohort (median 1 line).

All patients had prior exposure to chemotherapy. Furthermore, 53.8% of the total population had previously received CDK4/6 inhibitors. Consistent with the difference in treatment lines, prior CDK4/6 inhibitor exposure was substantially higher in the Q4W cohort (90.9%) compared to the Q3W cohort (26.7%). Conversely, regarding specific prior chemotherapies, 8 patients (30.8%) had previously received capecitabine, with a substantially higher proportion observed in the Q3W cohort compared to the Q4W cohort (40.0% vs. 18.2%). This difference clinically reflects the higher proportion of HR-positive patients in the Q4W cohort (as evidenced by their extensive prior CDK4/6 inhibitor use), for whom cytotoxic agents like capecitabine are generally deferred in favor of sequential endocrine-based therapies.

sec.title: Dose escalation and DLTs
sec.p:
Dose escalation was conducted using a standard 3 + 3 design, 26 patients were enrolled alternately into the Q3W and Q4W cohorts. No DLTs were observed during the DLT observation period (Cycle 1) in any cohort, and the MTD was not reached within the tested dose ranges. The treatment duration, dose levels, and best overall response for each patient across the dose-escalation cohorts are visualized in Fig. 2.Fig. 2

The dose level is also indicated by the color of the horizontal bars. Each horizontal bar represents an individual patient, ordered by treatment duration within each dose group. In the Q3W (N = 15) cohort, dose escalation proceeded from 16 mg/m2 to the pre-specified dose level of 22 mg/m2. Since no DLTs were observed during the first cycle at 22 mg/m2, the dose was further escalated to 24 mg/m2 (enrolling 2 patients), while one additional patient was backfilled into the 22 mg/m2 group. Although the criteria for DLTs (typically assessed in Cycle 1) were not met, further enrollment at the 24 mg/m2 level was halted because patients experienced ≥Grade 3 adverse events (AEs) in subsequent treatment cycles, suggesting potential cumulative toxicity at this higher dose intensity.

In the Q4W (N = 11) cohort, the dose was escalated from 16 mg/m2 up to 22 mg/m2. Notably, a minor protocol adjustment was made at the 16 mg/m2 dose level, where one fewer patient was enrolled than planned. This decision was driven by the slow recruitment rate and the urgent clinical need for effective therapy in this heavily pre-treated population with late-line disease. Importantly, this adjustment was supported by concurrent safety data from the Q3W cohort, which had already demonstrated a favorable safety profile at the higher dose of 18 mg/m2 without DLTs.

sec.p:

Hematological toxicities were the most common Grade 3 or 4 events. Neutropenia and leukopenia were the most frequently reported hematological TRAEs, each occurring in 80.8% (21/26) of patients. Grade 3/4 neutropenia and leukopenia were both observed in 50.0% (13/26) of patients. Notably, these Grade 3 or 4 hematological toxicities typically occurred in later treatment cycles (median onset: Cycle 3–4), suggesting a cumulative effect. However, these events were transient and effectively managed with supportive care, including granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and dose modifications, allowing most patients to continue treatment. No cases of febrile neutropenia were reported. Other hematological TRAEs, such as anemia (26.9%) and thrombocytopenia (26.9%), were mostly Grade 1 or 2.

Regarding non-hematological toxicities, skin hyperpigmentation was the most common adverse event, occurring in 76.9% (20/26) of patients. This phenomenon, characterized by a reversible blue discoloration of the skin typical of liposomal mitoxantrone, was exclusively Grade 1 or 2 and did not lead to treatment discontinuation. Other common non-hematological TRAEs included fatigue (61.5%), anorexia (53.8%), and hand-foot syndrome (50.0%). While most non-hematological events were mild to moderate, Grade 3 hand-foot syndrome was observed in 5 patients (19.2%) and was managed through dose interruptions or reductions. Interstitial lung disease (ILD) was reported in 19.2% (5/26) of patients, distributed across various dose levels without a clear dose-dependent pattern. Diagnoses were established via high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) combined with the clinical exclusion of infectious etiologies. Most cases (n = 4) were asymptomatic Grade 1 and managed conservatively with dose reductions and intensified monitoring. One patient experienced symptomatic Grade 2 ILD, which was effectively managed with dose interruption and systemic corticosteroids. Importantly, all ILD events were fully reversible, did not progress to Grade ≥ 3, and did not lead to definitive treatment discontinuation. Other sporadic Grade 2 events included hypersensitivity (infusion reaction) and blurred vision, each reported in one patient (3.8%). No Grade 4 non-hematological TRAEs or treatment-related deaths were recorded.

Given the historical cardiotoxicity associated with anthracenediones, cardiac safety was rigorously evaluated as a special interest. Notably, 76.9% (n = 20) of the enrolled patients had prior exposure to conventional anthracyclines. Per protocol, all these patients were rigorously screened to ensure their historical cumulative anthracycline doses were strictly below the established cardiotoxic safety thresholds (i.e., doxorubicin ≤ 350 mg/m² or epirubicin ≤ 700 mg/m²) with a confirmed baseline LVEF ≥ 50%. Under the rigorous cardiovascular surveillance protocol, the median cardiac follow-up duration for the study cohort was 4.1 months. The absolute minimum cardiac follow-up duration was 0.7 months for the patient with the shortest treatment exposure (accounting for active treatment plus the mandated End of Treatment evaluation), while the maximum extended up to 13.9 months. During this period, the combination demonstrated an exceptionally favorable cardiac safety profile. Longitudinal echocardiographic monitoring showed no declines in LVEF and no cases of congestive heart failure. Furthermore, routine ECGs and cardiac biomarkers (troponin/BNP) remained stable throughout treatment. While one patient exhibited an elevated NT-proBNP level, cardiological consultation confirmed the elevation was present at baseline and was not related to the study medication. No treatment-emergent cardiac events required dose modification or discontinuation.

The safety profiles were generally comparable between the Q3W (n = 15) and Q4W (n = 11) cohorts, with no new safety signals observed in either group (Table 3). The incidence of Grade 3/4 neutropenia was numerically higher in the Q4W cohort compared to the Q3W cohort (63.6% vs. 40.0%), likely reflecting the higher dose intensity and heavy pretreatment in the Q4W group. Regarding treatment exposure, the median cumulative Lipo-MIT exposure was 84.0 mg/m² (range, 16.0–120.0) in the Q3W cohort and 130.0 mg/m² (range, 35.0–220.0) in the Q4W cohort. The median relative dose intensity (RDI) was 86.3% (range, 44.9% – 100.0%) for the Q3W schedule and 91.3% (range, 51.8%–100.0%) for the Q4W schedule. Dose interruptions (delays > 7 days) due to adverse events occurred in 40.0% of patients in the Q3W cohort and 45.5% in the Q4W cohort. Dose reductions were required in 53.3% (8/15) of patients in the Q3W cohort and 63.6% (7/11) in the Q4W cohort. Interestingly, while the Q4W cohort had a higher rate of dose reductions, it demonstrated a substantially lower rate of treatment discontinuation due to TRAEs (18.2%) compared to the Q3W cohort (66.7%). This suggests that the Q4W schedule, combined with active dose management, enabled better long-term tolerability and treatment persistence in this advanced patient population.

sec.p:

The investigator-assessed ORR for the total population was 23.1% (6/26; 95% CI, 9.0%–43.6%), and the DCR was 80.8% (21/26; 95% CI, 60.6%–93.4%). In a post hoc, exploratory analysis, when stratified by dosing schedule, the Q4W cohort demonstrated a numerically higher response rate and disease control compared to the Q3W cohort. Specifically, the ORR was 36.4% (4/11) in the Q4W cohort versus 13.3% (2/15) in the Q3W cohort. Similarly, the DCR was notably higher in the Q4W cohort (90.9%; 10/11) compared to the Q3W cohort (73.3%; 11/15). Importantly, prior capecitabine exposure appeared to influence the depth of response. Among the 8 capecitabine-pretreated patients, no partial responses were observed, although 6 achieved stable disease (DCR 75.0%). Consequently, all 6 PRs occurred in patients without prior capecitabine exposure.

Changes in target lesion size were further visualized. The waterfall plot (Fig. 3B) highlights the best percentage change in target lesion size from baseline, showing that a greater proportion of patients in the Q4W cohort achieved deep tumor regression exceeding the − 30% threshold required for PR. The spider plot (Fig. 3C) illustrates the longitudinal changes in tumor burden over time. In this post hoc, exploratory evaluation, there appeared to be a numerical trend toward deeper responses in the Q4W cohort, with several patients maintaining tumor shrinkage for an extended period.Fig. 3

A post hoc, exploratory survival analysis demonstrated a numerically longer progression-free survival for patients receiving the Q4W dosing schedule (Fig. 3A). At the time of analysis, a total of 18 PFS events (disease progression or death) had occurred across the overall population. The median PFS (mPFS) for the total population was 6.6 months (95% CI, 4.7–NR). Notably, the Q4W cohort (7 PFS events, 63.6%) achieved a median PFS of 12.7 months (95% CI, 9.3–NR), with 6-month and 12-month PFS rates of 72.7% and 53.0%, respectively. This was numerically longer than the median PFS observed in the Q3W cohort (11 PFS events, 73.3%), which was 5.4 months (95% CI, 4.7–NR) with 6-month and 12-month PFS rates of 37.7% and 18.9%, respectively.

Given the baseline imbalances between the Q3W and Q4W cohorts, a post hoc, exploratory multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression model was performed. After adjusting for hormone receptor status, prior CDK4/6 inhibitor exposure, and the number of prior lines of therapy, the Q4W dosing schedule yielded a numerically lower risk of disease progression compared with the Q3W schedule, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.41 (95% CI, 0.11–1.49; p = 0.175) (Additional file 1: Table S1). Other clinical variables did not show statistically significant associations with PFS in this limited sample size.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our phase I dose-escalation study represents the first clinical investigation exploring the combination of Lipo-MIT and capecitabine in patients with pretreated HER2-negative ABC. We successfully established the RP2D as Lipo-MIT 22 mg/m2 administered every 4 weeks (Q4W) combined with standard capecitabine. At this dose level, the regimen demonstrated a manageable safety profile and preliminary antitumor activity, with an ORR of 36.4% and a mPFS of 12.7 months in the Q4W cohort. These findings suggest that revitalizing a classic cytotoxic agent through advanced nanotechnology offers a promising therapeutic strategy for patients who have exhausted standard anthracyclines and taxanes [17].

The therapeutic landscape for HER2-negative ABC, comprising both HR + and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), remains challenging in the later-line setting [18]. For HR+/HER2- patients, resistance inevitably develops after CDK4/6 inhibitors and subsequent targeted endocrine therapies (e.g., PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitors or oral selective estrogen receptor degraders [SERDs]), leaving chemotherapy as the primary salvage option [19, 20]. Similarly, patients with TNBC face a dismal prognosis with limited options after progression on first-line chemo-immunotherapy (e.g., for PD-L1–positive disease) or modern antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) like sacituzumab govitecan and datopotamab deruxtecan [21–23]. Importantly, given that 61.5% of patients in our study had HER2-low disease, the paradigm-shifting advent of ADCs (most notably trastuzumab deruxtecan) must be contextualized [24]. While ADCs rightfully represent the standard of care in earlier lines for HER2-low ABC, the Lipo-MIT plus capecitabine regimen may serve as a potential and accessible later-line option for patients who have exhausted ADC therapies, are ineligible due to specific toxicities (e.g., ILD), or face socioeconomic barriers. In this context, conventional chemotherapy (e.g., gemcitabine, vinorelbine, or single-agent capecitabine) provides limited survival benefit, with historical median PFS typically ranging from 4 to 6 months [16, 24]. Our study addresses this urgent unmet need by providing a “gentle yet durable” chemotherapy alternative. The median PFS of 12.7 months observed in our Q4W cohort compares favorably with historical controls, potentially delaying the need for more toxic regimens and preserving quality of life.

Mitoxantrone, a synthetic anthracenedione, was historically a potent weapon in the oncologist’s arsenal. Its mechanism involves DNA intercalation causing strand breaks and inhibition of topoisomerase II, along with a unique capacity to suppress B-cell, T-cell, and macrophage proliferation, thereby modulating the immune microenvironment [5, 25, 26]. However, its clinical utility—particularly in breast cancer—was marginalized due to cumulative cardiotoxicity and dose-limiting myelosuppression [7]. The development of Lipo-MIT marks a paradigm shift. Unlike the free drug, Lipo-MIT utilizes a pegylated liposomal delivery system with a “golden mean” particle size of approximately 60 nm. This specific dimension is critical: it is large enough to prevent extravasation through the tight junctions of normal capillaries (2–8 nm), thereby shielding healthy tissues such as the myocardium and skin from toxic exposure [27] yet, it is small enough to effectively extravasate through the leaky vasculature of tumors (300–500 nm) via the EPR effect [11]. However, it is acknowledged that the clinical translation of EPR-dependent delivery can be variable due to the profound heterogeneity of human tumor vasculature and dense stromal barriers. Furthermore, the “stealth” PEG coating evades detection by the reticuloendothelial system (RES), extending the plasma half-life to approximately 90 h [12]. Our initial data support this design rationale: the combination was well-tolerated, with a notable absence of severe short-term cardiac events and Hand-Foot Syndrome. In the current clinical landscape, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD) remains a standard option [28]. However, Lipo-MIT may serve as a complementary alternative, particularly for patients who have reached their lifetime cumulative dose limits for traditional anthracyclines, offering a potential “re-challenge” strategy with a distinct toxicity profile (e.g., lower rates of severe palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia typically associated with PLD) [29, 30].

Regarding non-hematological toxicities, the 19.2% (n = 5) incidence of ILD represents a non-negligible safety signal that warrants balanced contextualization. In the current era of advanced breast cancer therapy, where ADC-associated pneumonitis has emerged as a paramount clinical concern, this finding requires careful interpretation. Mechanistically, this class effect may be driven by the prolonged circulation and alveolar macrophage uptake inherent to pegylated liposomes [31]. Critically, however, the clinical profile observed in our study was distinct from the potentially severe pneumonitis associated with certain novel ADCs; all ILD events were exclusively low-grade (Grade 1–2) and fully reversible, with no patient requiring definitive treatment discontinuation. Nevertheless, given the potential risk, proactive high-resolution CT (HRCT) surveillance and early intervention remain mandatory for all future trials evaluating Lipo-MIT-based regimens.

While contemporary guidelines favor sequential single-agent chemotherapy to preserve quality of life, combination regimens remain crucial for rapid disease control; therefore, we leveraged the liposomal formulation to safely harness the potential synergistic effect of mitoxantrone and capecitabine. The rationale for combining Lipo-MIT with capecitabine is further supported by comparing our results with the phase II study of Lipo-MIT monotherapy conducted by Wang et al. [13]. In their study, Lipo-MIT monotherapy demonstrated encouraging efficacy in advanced breast cancer. However, the objective response rate and progression-free survival observed in our combination cohort (Q4W: ORR 36.4%, median PFS 12.7 months) appear numerically higher than those reported for the single-agent regimen. While indirect, this exploratory comparison raises the hypothesis of a potential synergistic effect between the DNA-damaging anthraquinone and the antimetabolite fluoropyrimidine. Mechanistically, mitoxantrone-induced DNA strand breaks may modulate the enzymes involved in fluorouracil metabolism or inhibit repair pathways, thereby sensitizing tumor cells to capecitabine [32]. This synergistic hypothesis is clinically supported by our observation that durable disease control was still achieved in patients with prior capecitabine exposure. Furthermore, our established RP2D of 22 mg/m2 aligns well with the tolerable therapeutic window identified in previous monotherapy trials, optimizing the balance between synergistic efficacy and overlapping toxicities (such as myelosuppression).

An important exploratory observation from this study is the differential tolerability and efficacy outcomes of the Q4W dosing schedule compared to the conventional Q3W regimen. While standard chemotherapy often relies on 3-weekly cycles, the known historical pharmacokinetics of Lipo-MIT demanded a tailored approach. Conceptually, we hypothesized that the extended 4-week dosing interval might better align with its known prolonged circulation time (~ 90 h), potentially mitigating overlapping hematological toxicities observed clinically while maintaining adequate tumor drug exposure [12]. However, comprehensive PK and PK-PD analyses for the current study cohort are ongoing and will be reported separately. In the absence of these formal, trial-specific PK-PD correlations, the definitive attribution of the observed efficacy or tolerability differences to specific pharmacokinetic parameters remains a hypothesis and should be interpreted with appropriate caution. Clinically, this hypothesized advantage was supported by the numerically higher ORR (36.4% vs. 13.3%) and numerically longer median PFS (12.7 vs. 5.4 months) in the Q4W cohort compared to Q3W. Beyond the potential pharmacokinetic advantages of Lipo-MIT, the differential capecitabine exposure between the cohorts (1000 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–14 in Q3W versus 825 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–21 in Q4W) must be considered as a critical independent variable. Mechanistically, the prolonged administration of capecitabine at a lower dose in the Q4W schedule may exert a metronomic-like effect. Such continuous, low-dose exposure is hypothesized to enhance anti-angiogenic activity and favorably modulate the tumor immune microenvironment [33]. This metronomic dynamic could synergize effectively with the known macrophage-suppressive properties of mitoxantrone, thereby independently contributing to the deeper and more durable disease control observed in the Q4W cohort [5, 25, 26].

Because the MTD was not reached, the RP2D was determined through holistic clinical judgment rather than traditional dose-limiting toxicity rules. This decision was primarily driven by the evaluation of cumulative toxicity and overall treatment exposure. Specifically, the Q3W regimen led to an unsustainable rate of treatment discontinuation due to cumulative myelosuppression. In contrast, the extended Q4W interval provided adequate hematopoietic recovery time, preserved overall dose intensity, and prolonged safe treatment exposure. Consequently, balancing sustained tolerability with efficacy, Lipo-MIT 22 mg/m² Q4W combined with capecitabine was established as the RP2D. Of particular clinical significance is the regimen’s performance in patients with prior CDK4/6 inhibitor exposure. In the Q4W cohort, 90.9% of patients had progressed on prior CDK4/6 inhibitors, a population known to harbor resistance mechanisms that often render subsequent conventional chemotherapy less effective. Despite this heavy pretreatment, the combination achieved a median PFS of 12.7 months. This exploratory finding implies that Lipo-MIT combined with capecitabine might offer a viable clinical option for patients with prior CDK4/6 inhibitor exposure, though this hypothesis requires validation in larger cohorts.

We acknowledge several limitations in our study. First, as a non-randomized phase I trial with a small sample size (N = 26; Q4W n = 11) and lacking prospectively defined quantitative criteria for RP2D determination when the MTD is not reached, the study was not powered for inter-cohort efficacy comparisons. Crucially, because the Q3W and Q4W cohorts were enrolled sequentially rather than concurrently, any efficacy comparisons between these schedules are strictly exploratory and hypothesis-generating. These exploratory comparisons are heavily confounded by inherent differences in capecitabine dosing intensity (d1-14 in Q3W vs. d1-21 in Q4W), substantial imbalances in prior treatment exposures (e.g., prior CDK4/6 inhibitor use, and 40.0% vs. 18.2% prior capecitabine exposure), and overall baseline patient characteristics. Therefore, the numerical differences observed should be interpreted with extreme caution, which is further reflected by the non-significant log-rank p-value and wide overlapping confidence intervals. Due to sample size constraints, not all confounding variables could be incorporated into the multivariable Cox model. Additionally, this exploratory model is limited by a low events-per-variable ratio (18 events for 3 covariates), introducing a potential risk of statistical overfitting; thus, the adjusted hazard ratio is statistically fragile. Finally, the markedly higher rate of treatment discontinuation due to adverse events in the Q3W cohort (66.7% vs. 18.2% in Q4W) raises the potential for informative censoring. Although our progression-free survival analysis strictly followed the intention-to-treat principle, patients who discontinued therapy early due to toxicity may have had altered subsequent follow-up or disease trajectories, potentially biasing the Kaplan-Meier estimates.

Second, tumor responses were determined by investigator assessment without an independent central radiologic review, introducing potential evaluation bias. Third, we did not collect tumor tissue to mechanistically confirm the hypothesized immune-modulating synergy. Finally, although the short-term cardiac safety data are reassuring, the limited duration of our current cardiac follow-up precludes the detection of late-onset cardiotoxicity; therefore, longer-term cardiac monitoring remains essential to fully characterize the long-term cardiac profile of Lipo-MIT [34]. Future randomized Phase II/III trials are warranted to definitively evaluate the efficacy of the Q4W regimen, specifically comparing Lipo-MIT plus capecitabine against treatment of physician’s choice (TPC) chemotherapy, with PFS as the primary endpoint, in patients with pretreated HER2-negative ABC (e.g., post-CDK4/6 inhibitors and/or post-ADC).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This phase I dose-escalation study successfully establishes Lipo-MIT 22 mg/m2 administered every 4 weeks combined with capecitabine as the RP2D for patients with pretreated HER2-negative ABC. The regimen demonstrated a manageable safety profile, which may help mitigate the historical cardiotoxicity and cumulative myelosuppression associated with conventional anthracyclines. Furthermore, the preliminary efficacy signal—highlighted by a mPFS of 12.7 months in the Q4W cohort—raises the hypothesis of a potential synergistic effect compared with historical single-agent chemotherapy controls. Our findings support a nanotechnology-enabled strategy to revitalize classic chemotherapeutics, warranting further confirmation in large-scale randomized trials.
